text: Aalto's humanoid robot, Väiski, can do a backflip. Ask it to put three blocks into three boxes, and it is lost.
So we gave it a brain. Box. Off. Ice. Box Office.
Three to five objects lie on the counter. Three boxes, two minutes. A right box earns points. A wrong box costs one. So when it is unsure, it skips.
You tell it where things go, in your own words. The blue ones in between. The first box from the left. No templates.

Under the hood, the head camera finds each object and its shape. A parser turns the sentence into a box for each object. Aalto's own planner moves the arm, and every move is checked against the safety filter before it runs.

Aalto's real recordings showed us the trap. Standard colour rules saw the orange boxes and the robot's own hands as objects. Box Office finds the real ones, and levels a camera that was tilted by fourteen degrees.

In Aalto's simulator, on randomised scenes, it sorted ten of twenty objects on the fixed task, up from eight, and ten of eighteen by instruction. Not one object went into a wrong box. The safety filter never clipped a command.
And on the real recordings, it starts moving after one second, not fifty-two.
The hardest part was not the brain. It was the fingers. A few millimetres of camera error, and a round object slips away. That is what we fix next.
Box Office. Plain words in, sorted boxes out. Built at Junction twenty twenty-six.
